title: S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models
summary: Typed System-1 (S1) decision models are increasingly deployed in LLM agents for routing, moderation, and authorization to cut inference cost, yet untrusted context can still manipulate typed outputs and alter execution branches. Unlike autoregressive System-2 (S2) models, S1 interfaces score dynamic rules and options without token-by-token decoding, mismatching attacks targeting text continuation or explicit override commands. We propose S1-Evo, a self-evolving framework tailored to S1's contract-based option competition and margin feedback. S1-Evo perturbs untrusted fields via contract-aware evidence channels to induce \emph{evidence competition} with original task evidence while preserving fact invariance. Offline on seed tasks, it optimizes candidates via feedback search guided by directional margins and re-verification, distilling verified flips into experience cards. At test time, S1-Evo retrieves relevant cards to construct perturbations for unseen tasks. Across four benchmarks and three S1 models, S1-Evo reaches 71.99\% mean ASR and 57.47\% high-confidence ASR on \texttt{jev-1.14}, and causes up to 24.00\% E2E agent violations.

title: AgentSSL: Can MLE Agents Leverage Unlabeled Data?
summary: Applying machine learning systems to new domains introduces bottlenecks in both labeled data acquisition and manual pipeline engineering. While recent MLE agents show promise in automating pipeline design, they have been studied almost exclusively in fully supervised settings, leaving them untested in realistic regimes where labeled data is scarce but unlabeled data is abundant. In this work, we introduce Agentic Semi-Supervised Learning (AgentSSL), framing SSL as a program search problem and studying how agents navigate this space under limited supervision. We find that even under weak feedback and matched compute, agents can synthesize code that combines and adapts established SSL techniques, exceeding the strongest human-engineered baselines in 8 of 12 settings by up to +21.8%. However, our results identify program selection as a critical bottleneck in AgentSSL, where performance drops by as much as 47% when selecting based on the agent's feedback metric. To systematically study this bottleneck, we introduce ProgramSelectBench, a large-scale benchmark with a combined total of 16,977 agent-generated and human-engineered SSL programs, and evaluate both unsupervised and active program selection methods. We further evaluate AgentSSL on real-world ecology detection tasks, highlighting the opportunities and challenges of transferring agent-discovered strategies beyond controlled benchmarks.

title: From Delegation to Coordination: Learning Efficient Multi-Agent Deep Research
summary: Multi-agent deep-research systems use delegation to parallelize search and keep long tool traces out of the main agent's context. Yet delegation helps only when task allocation and subtask execution are coordinated: the main agent must issue useful subtasks, while subagents must return reliable evidence. Existing training either optimizes only the main agent or broadcasts the same team advantage to all agents, which can reward misleading subagent reports and penalize useful ones. We introduce LEAD-RL (Learning Effective Agent Delegation with Reinforcement Learning), a joint main-agent-subagent training framework with contribution-aware credit assignment. A training-time rubric evaluates the research utility of each subagent report and gates its inherited team advantage, while final-answer correctness remains the only team reward; no token, step, or speedup reward is used. Across five benchmarks and two model families, LEAD-RL improves answer quality. On BrowseComp, it improves accuracy by 2.49 percentage points and reduces critical-path cost by 24.5% over joint training with shared team credit. During validation, accuracy increases by 6.78 points at approximately constant critical-path cost. These results show that contribution-aware credit assignment improves the quality-efficiency trade-off of multi-agent deep research.

title: llm-gemini 0.37
summary:
Release: llm-gemini 0.37

Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen today - the lowest cost member of the Gemini 4 family.

It's actually not too far off the price of its much bigger siblings, Carbon and Argon. I'm finding Gemini 4's pricing really confusing. Here's the pricing scheme:

Model Dates Input ($/M) Cached input Output
Gemini 4 Carbon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00
From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00
Gemini 4 Argon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00
From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00
Gemini 4 Hydrogen   $1.50 $0.075 $7.50

Carbon and Argon are the same price, and both are scheduled to double in price on December 1st. If they're the same price, why have two different models? Google says that Argon "delivers Gemini 4 intelligence with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon" - so it may be priced the same, but it will use less tokens per task.

Hydrogen, supposedly the cheap model, is currently only a 25% discount on its more capable peers. The Hydrogen price will make more sense after December 1st, when it will represent a 75% discount. It's still considerably more expensive than Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna - they're both $0.10/$0.50, so Hydrogen is 15x that.

I had Hydrogen generate some pelicans. Here's a full comparison grid showing the pelicans for all three members of the Gemini 4 family at their three supported effort levels:

Considering how close they are in price, the difference in pelican quality for Hydrogen is quite stark.

Here's how Google describe Hydrogen's intended position in their mix of models:

In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows.

Most notably, Hydrogen is the new free tier model, and is the model that will power AI features in Google Search.

title: Building strong safety evaluations
summary: Recommendations for designing, running, and reporting safety evaluations, based on our own experiences.
story_key: story|title:building strong safety evaluations
content_excerpt: Safety evaluations inform some of the most consequential decisions we make about an AI model, including whether it’s ready to deploy, which safeguards ship alongside it, and what our next round of safety training and research should focus on. When we say a model is “safer than its predecessor,” we mean that it scored better on a set of evals someone built. But a safety claim is only as sound as the eval behind it, and good ones are hard to build. A safety eval measures a model’s propensity to cause or contribute to harm, whether its response to a request makes harm more or less likely, and how severe that harm would be, rather than measuring specific capabilities. It can cover different types of harm. For example, a user may actively request harmful outputs (such as seeking instructions on how to harm themselves), or they may request outputs that are intended to be harmless, but that come with high risk of unintended harm (such as seeking information on the appropriate dose of a drug). Essentially, a safety eval asks, “Given a specific input, did the model do the right thing?” Like other types of evals, these can be tricky to get right: researchers have repeatedly found that AI evals are easy to game , don’t always measure what they claim to measure, and aren’t documented well enough to reproduce . The results can change depending on whether the questions are multiple-choice or open-ended , or even based on how answer options are ordered . Psychology faced similar issues a decade ago, when large-scale replication projects found that many published findings didn’t hold up, likely at least in part because many original studies relied on small samples and journals favored statistically significant results. In response, the field instituted reforms such as preregistration (writing down hypotheses and analysis plans before collecting or analyzing data), better measurement, and more rigorous statistics, which made measurements more trustworthy and results easier to replicate. Drawing on those reforms, and from our experience building evals at Anthropic , 1 this post shares recommendations for anyone who builds or relies on AI safety evaluations, using examples from our system cards . title: Consistent Video-to-Video Translation via Explicit Correspondences
summary: Interactive video-to-video applications require real-time generation while maintaining long-range temporal consistency. However, recent methods achieve speed by restricting attention to a fixed-length causal window. This limits long-range consistency whenever relevant history falls outside the context window. To address this limitation, we introduce vid2vid-long, a correspondence-based approach grounded in a simple observation. Video-to-video translation provides an explicit cross-frame reference: the regions that match in the input video should match in the output video too. Concretely, we compute patch-level correspondences in the input, guiding retrieval of previously generated outputs in the corresponding regions, and condition the model on these patches through correspondence cross-attention. Our experiments demonstrate that vid2vid-long consistently improves long-range temporal consistency across recent video models while preserving generation quality and real-time performance.

On every occasion, we mentioned our commitment to open sourcing it so that developers could run their own browser engine on their own Cloudflare accounts if they want to. That promise is now real. Kitesurf is open source on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. You can read the code, run it locally, change it, and deploy your own instance to Cloudflare Workers. Read more about why and how we built Kitesurf in our initial announcement and how to use it in Browser Run’s developer documentation. Kitesurf has three main parts: the Engine manages browser sessions and client connections, PageScript runs the page and its JavaScript, and PageRenderer draws the result. Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity and life sciences research, available through our verification programs. If you build on the Claude Platform or work in Claude Code , you may be wondering which model to use for your common tasks. This article will help answer that question and how to think about the trade-offs. The quick answer is that you should start most work on Opus 5.5 at its default effort level, medium . There's a reason it's the default model in Claude Code. It costs half as much per input and output token as Fable 5.2, and it's the model we recommend starting with for most coding and knowledge work. Before you move models, try adjusting your effort level. It's a finer dial for both cost and capability. Past high , one more effort level can cost as much as a bigger model, so compare both on your own work. If you're past high , test the next model up at a lower effort instead. Conversely, one level down can get you the result you need at a lower rate. Higher effort helps when the model needs to think longer, call more tools, or check its own work more. Just keep in mind that it also adds latency. Additionally, moving to a higher effort level won't give a model knowledge or skill it doesn't have. For that, you still need to move up a model. Prices are Claude API list prices. For benchmark results, see the Fable 5.2 page . When you choose between models, you're making a trade-off. When you pick a larger model, for example, you are choosing capability over latency. These are the main trade-offs to think through. Generally, bigger models cost more per token and are more capable, but the cost vs capability trade-off isn't universally true at the task level. summary:
Anthropic's IPO roadshow video

Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works.

The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs.

I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below:

We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...]

As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention. Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...]

The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units.

Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack. We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself, allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster.

We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their postmortem of three recent issues, where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments.

  • Changed MCP_SDK_GENERATION=v1 to run the v2 MCP client in a compatibility mode (earlier handshake, relaxed OAuth sign-in checks), because the v1 MCP client is removed
  • Changed the tool Claude uses to finish an MCP server sign-in so that it asks you to confirm, even in bypass and auto modes; where nobody can be asked, such as in dontAsk mode, use /mcp
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed a session at a connector's approval prompt or sign-in inside a running tool to be released as paused at the idle or lifetime limit; a late answer resumes from a fresh clone
  • Changed artifact updates to ask first, even under an allow rule, when people outside your organization can see the artifact or Claude can't check who can
  • Changed glab config set without --global or --host, and glab config edit --local, to fail read-only inside the Bash sandbox; run them outside it
  • Changed the Bash sandbox on macOS, Linux and WSL to ignore write access granted through a symlink in a writable folder that leads elsewhere or to a missing path; grant the real path instead
  • Changed "don't ask again" so an allow rule that looks like it holds a secret, or would be saved to a settings.local.json that git tracks, lasts for the session only and isn't saved
  • Changed the sandbox on macOS and Linux: git worktree add, move and remove now fail read-only, as do commits in a worktree the session wasn't started in or given, even one inside the project
  • Changed start-up to stop when a --settings file isn't valid JSON and has a sandbox key, even one that turns the sandbox off
  • Changed what happens when a tool's permission check fails with an error after a PreToolUse hook returned "allow": Claude Code now decides the call as if no hook had answered
  • Changed what happens when a tool's permission check fails on input that a PermissionRequest hook rewrote: Claude Code now asks again, or refuses the call where nobody can answer
  • Changed the GitLab merge request badge to show only for the repository a sandboxed session opened in
  • Changed the claude mcp add --help example to a local command
  • Changed mods: a *, namespace or negated hook on engine.create now only observes. To add or withhold a $ noun, hook engine.create by name
  • Changed claude plugin validate to fail a mod whose engine.create hook isn't written in the one accepted form; installed mods keep loading
  • Changed marketplace and plugin installs to fail when a git submodule isn't on the commit its repository records
  • Changed project (.mcp.json) MCP server approvals to match the server's exact name; an approval entry written in another spelling now asks again
  • Changed self-hosted runners under --trust-workspace false and VS Code sessions in an untrusted folder: the repository's settings can no longer disable your hooks or turn plugins on or off
  • Changed tool.list plugin hooks so the tools they add or remove apply to the model and every agent
  • Changed claude plugin install and /plugin to show a warning instead of success when a plugin's install command writes to stderr
  • Changed claude.ai chats and Cowork tasks to check a plugin file for secret keys before sending it, and to ask first if it may hold one
  • Changed claude rm and the agents view to say a session is removed from the list, not deleted; claude rm help says the conversation is kept and claude --resume lists it
  • Changed /stickers to say that the sticker pack is all claimed for now, instead of opening a page in the browser
  • Changed a managed settings policyHelper to no longer take environment variables from user or --settings files; set what it needs in managed env or the launching shell
  • Changed a /skill or @file typed between two files picked in claude.ai or the desktop app, or after a picked file and a link, to no longer take effect
  • Changed split-pane agent teammates to check that requests come from their team lead: one that outlives its lead has its asks refused, and plan approvals must be re-sent after /clear or /resume
  • Changed worktree creation to refuse checkouts whose .git folders are links or hold hard links, such as git-new-workdir layouts and cp -al copies; use a plain clone
  • Changed what Claude is told after safeguards stop a forked skill or a workflow agent: retry with a narrower prompt or tell you, instead of doing the work itself
  • Changed browser tool calls (Claude in Chrome, the desktop browser pane) to refuse some escaped or JSON-text inputs and tell Claude how to respell them
  • Changed workflows so that a prompt an app marks as not typed no longer reaches their agents as your request
  • Changed computer use on macOS to refuse key chords that hold Space with Control or Option, and more system shortcuts that need your grant
  • Changed first-run setup in Terminal.app to name the "Use Option as Meta key" setting, what Option stops typing, and how to undo it before you agree
  • Changed the maximum of CLAUDE_CODE_OVERLOADED_RETRY_MAX_DELAY_MS from 64000 to 300000
  • Changed workflows in the desktop app's Code tab to pause at a usage limit and continue after it resets
  • Changed the spend limit and 1M context errors, and /usage-credits, in cloud sessions and under Remote Control: they no longer give a web address
  • Changed which MCP servers are reported by name in OpenTelemetry exports to follow the current connector directory
  • Changed /logout in a background session, which had no effect: it now signs out every session on the computer, deletes stored MCP logins and plugin secrets, and ends the session, as in a terminal
  • macOS: Changed the Bash sandbox so lsof and similar tools may show less about processes a command did not start
  • Changed cloud scheduled tasks: a PostToolUse hook from your own settings can no longer replace the plan in ExitPlanMode's result
  • Changed CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE in Anthropic-hosted cloud sessions to stop applying to auto-memory extraction and, in some sessions, to /btw; the main conversation still follows it
  • Removed the subagentStatusLine setting: subagent rows always use the default look, and settings files that still hold the key load as before
  • Deprecated a plugin's agent setting: it still applies, and now warns at startup, in claude plugin list and in claude plugin validate
  • [VSCode] Added a Claude Code trust prompt before the first session in a folder you haven't trusted; declining leaves the folder's settings and MCP servers unused
  • [VSCode] Added the live output of a running Bash or PowerShell command to the chat, under the command's card
  • [VSCode] Fixed a response that was discarded because its tool call could not be parsed still showing after Claude retried
  • [VSCode] Fixed a queued message missing from a conversation or fork when it directly followed a compaction summary
  • [VSCode] Fixed the "Buy usage credits on claude.ai" button counting as agreement to pay for Fable while usage credits were off
  • [VSCode] Fixed the "extensions want to relaunch the terminal" warning coming back on open terminals after every window reload or restart
  • [VSCode] Fixed "Couldn't load this conversation's saved history" appearing in a new chat whose Claude process had restarted before the first prompt
  • [VSCode] Fixed the sign-in screen showing the login choices again after a pasted code; it now shows "Signing in…" until the sign-in finishes
  • [VSCode] Fixed the "You've hit your Fable limit" line staying in the VS Code and JetBrains panels after you pick another model
  • [VSCode] Fixed the Fable usage warning in the VS Code and JetBrains panels naming usage credits when they're off or used up
  • [VSCode] Fixed the diff tab not opening for multi-line edits on files with CRLF line endings
  • [VSCode] Fixed dictation continuing to record after switching sessions
  • [VSCode] Improved sign-in errors behind TLS-inspecting proxies: a certificate failure now says what to do, as the terminal does
  • [VSCode] Changed opening a Claude Code on the web session in a folder where Claude Code's sandbox is on: the extension no longer switches to the session's branch for you, and the dialog says why
  • [Claude Code on the web] Improved the message when a file fails to upload to a cloud or Remote Control session: it now gives the reason, such as too many pages, a password or a time-out
  • [Claude Code on the web] Improved adding a repository Claude can't access to a cloud session: a short message and a Reconnect GitHub button replace the long error
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed self-hosted sessions staying on "Starting Claude Code" after it had started, when you reopened a paused session without sending a message
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed a paused session in a self-hosted environment sometimes still showing "Sending" and a Stop button under the "Session paused" banner
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed pull request updates from GitHub Enterprise Server linking to github.com in cloud sessions; new updates link to your own server
  • [Claude Code on the web] Improved the message when some network secrets can't be added to a new cloud environment: it lists each host, says why where it can, and stays until you dismiss it
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed very large GitHub Actions job logs and run log archives failing to download or being cut off in cloud sessions
  • [Claude Code on the web] Improved the new-session repository picker when GitHub single sign-on hides organizations: it now says so even with other repositories listed, and links to reconnect GitHub
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed new cloud sessions started from the iOS app with a repository not getting a branch of their own
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed an open cloud or Remote Control session's page staying "Disconnected" after a few minutes of failed connections; it now tries to reconnect by itself
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed Try again on an open cloud or Remote Control session's "Connection lost" card sending "Try again" as your message; it now tries to reconnect instead
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed the Stop button disappearing from a cloud session five minutes into a reply that had shown nothing yet while Claude was still working
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed an approval prompt sometimes disappearing from a tab left open after a self-hosted runner released the session while it waited for your answer
  • [Claude Code on the web] Added a failure notification when a scheduled task's run can't start because its settings require a sandbox that isn't available where it runs
  • [Claude Code on the web] Improved the Git providers page when your GitHub sign-in has expired: it now asks you to reconnect instead of silently hiding organizations you can link
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed removing a repository from a scheduled task silently moving its GitHub trigger to another repository; Save now waits until you pick one
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed git clones and fetches that take longer than ten minutes in a cloud session sometimes being cut off at the very end
  • [Claude Code on the web] Added the No repository option to the repository picker for new sessions on a self-hosted environment
  • [Claude Code on the web] Added a warning to a cloud session's Delete dialog when deleting it will pause scheduled tasks that run in that session
  • [Remote Control] Fixed your own session saying its environment was deleted when you deleted nothing; it now says your computer is no longer connected
  • [Remote Control] Fixed some sessions still showing as running in the session list after the computer disconnected before Claude started; they now show an error mark or as idle
  • [Remote Control] Added a Try again button to the error shown when the computer running your session is signed out of Claude Code
  • [Claude Tag] Added Claude Tag sessions started in Slack to the Compliance API on Enterprise plans, in beta: list the sessions and read their transcripts
  • [Claude Tag] Added a confirmation step when an admin turns off Claude Tag for the organization, with a dialog that says what stops
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed scheduled tasks in a Slack channel moved between Enterprise Grid workspaces failing to use Slack until someone posted there
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed the Approve and post card in a DM with Claude appearing for private or Slack Connect channels, where Claude can't post; Claude now gets the reason and shows no card
  • [Claude Tag] Added a Retry button to a Slack channel's Configure page for when its settings fail to load
  • [Claude Tag] Added a Scope filter to the Network events tab of Claude Tag's Activity page, so admins can download one scope's events instead of the whole organization's
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Remove connector in Claude Tag admin settings being refused when access bundles also held its credentials; it now removes those set on the connector and leaves the bundles' own
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed the Channels tab in Claude Tag admin settings splitting a workspace from its channels across pages; channels now appear right under their workspace
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed the Set for Claude Tag link on the Cloud environments admin page not leading to the environment setting; it now opens the Slack page's Advanced tab, where you set it
  • [Code Review] Added a Download CSV button to Code Review admin settings: export review costs per repository by month, week or day, for one repository, one GitHub organization or all
